title: Keeping the Breath in Mind & Lessons in Samadhi
author: Ajaan Lee Dhammadharo
edition_cited: Third edition, 1990, printed for free distribution (archive.org OCR, item 'breathmind')
tradition: Thai forest tradition (Kammatthana), Ajaan Lee's breath method
locator_hints: Translator's introduction (file line c. 161): 'Signs and visions ... Some people experience them, others don't ... not really essential'

Method 1 (file line c. 826-892): breath spread in the head; 'a pale, murky vapor, or your own skull'; how to make a nimitta go away; expanding the 'bright white nimitta' to the size of the head, bringing it to 'The Fifth Base, the center of the chest', spreading breath and light to every pore; the 'brilliantly white ball or lump of light' produced at will

Lessons in Samadhi, the 'guests' passage (line c. 1183-1225): signs as bright lights, people, sounds, smells; controlling them by making them small, large, far, near (patibhaga nimitta) or else having nothing to do with them
Later talk (line c. 2185-2220): a vision arises and how discernment treats it
summary: Ajaan Lee's two breath-meditation methods with a set of talks. In Method 1 the meditator counts and then drops the count, lets breath sensation spread through the head and body, and is told that at this point signs may arise: tingling, 'a pale, murky vapor', one's own skull. An unwanted sign is dismissed by breathing long and deep into the heart. A wanted one is taken up one at a time: the bright white nimitta is enlarged to the size of the head, lowered to the centre of the chest, made 'as white and as bright as possible', and spread with the breath through the whole body. With mastery the 'brilliantly white ball or lump of light' can be produced at will and used as a field in which knowledge or pictures appear. The talks class lights, figures, sounds and smells as 'guests' to be brought under control or left alone; the translator notes that some meditators never experience them.
why_relevant: Thai forest instruction on what to do with a white light arising from breath practice (enlarge, relocate, brighten, spread), with the tradition's cautions and the explicit statement that the light is not essential.
